level: In-depth engineering course · no official exam
name: LLM Application Engineering
audience: Software engineers and architects building production LLM features, RAG systems and agents, alone or in small teams.
format: This site's course with a 40-question practice test of design, debugging, evaluation and cost questions across providers.
scenarios: Shipping a support assistant with RAG
Building an agent with tools and MCP
Cutting LLM cost and latency in half
Setting up evals before a model upgrade
Defending an app against prompt injection
verifyNotes: This is the site's own in-depth engineering course, not a vendor certification: there are no exam facts to confirm, so spend Research on finding the best official/primary sources per topic (URLs that will be cited as sources) and on what is current as of November 2026. Goal: a senior engineer or architect who builds products alone or in a team of 2-3 can apply every idea confidently in real work, a design review or a senior interview. Lessons go deep: intuition first, then the precise mechanism, then a fully worked example with real numbers or code, then where it matters in production, then a common misconception. Write math in LaTeX between double dollars only: $$...$$; NEVER single-dollar math (single $ renders literally; in SQL or shell code use code fences). In JSON strings escape backslashes. Markdown tables: never put a raw | inside a cell (escape it as \\| or use \\lvert in math). Every lesson has a hands-on lab: a small exercise with the expected output. State any randomness seed. Question mix: ~45% design and judgment in a concrete scenario, ~25% compute (token and cost estimates, cache savings, retrieval metrics like recall@k, MRR and nDCG, eval statistics), ~30% debugging (bad retrieval, tool-loop bugs, judge bias, injection). Code in fenced ```python blocks; verifiers run every computation and code question with /Users/ashotpahlevanyan/MyProjects/maark/claude-cert/web/.pipeline/py313/bin/python (CPython 3.13, standard library only; no network: code that calls an LLM API must be checked by reading the official SDK docs, never by guessing methods). Stay provider-neutral and show official SDK patterns of Anthropic, OpenAI and Google exactly as their docs show them; never invent API fields. Prices, model names, context sizes and limits change fast: state them conceptually or with an 'as of November 2026' note backed by a source. Sources: docs.claude.com / docs.anthropic.com, anthropic.com engineering and research posts, platform.openai.com docs and openai.com, ai.google.dev, modelcontextprotocol.io, genai.owasp.org, opentelemetry.io, github.com/pgvector/pgvector, arxiv.org primary papers, python.org; no Medium or vendor-marketing blogs of third parties.

domains.name: Model APIs, prompting and structured output
skills: Messages APIs across providers: roles, system prompts, multi-turn state, stop reasons
Prompt engineering that holds up: clear instructions, examples, XML/sections, prefill, chain of thought and extended thinking
Structured outputs: JSON Schema, strict modes, validation with Pydantic and repair strategies
Tokens and context windows: counting, budgeting, long-context trade-offs and context rot
Model choice and routing: capability vs cost vs latency tiers, fallbacks across providers

domains.name: Retrieval and RAG
skills: RAG architecture: ingestion, chunking strategies, metadata, and when RAG beats long context or fine-tuning
Embeddings: what they capture, normalisation, dimensions, choosing and versioning a model
Search: vector indexes (HNSW), BM25 and hybrid search with reciprocal rank fusion, filters
Reranking, query rewriting and contextual retrieval
Evaluating retrieval: recall@k, precision@k, MRR, nDCG, and building a labelled set

domains.name: Tools, agents and MCP
skills: The tool-use loop: tool definitions, tool results, parallel tool calls, turn limits and errors
Workflows vs agents: prompt chaining, routing, parallelisation, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer
Designing good tools: names, descriptions, inputs, output size, idempotency and least privilege
Model Context Protocol: hosts, clients and servers; tools, resources and prompts; transports and authorization
Context engineering for agents: memory, summarisation and compaction, sub-agents, and long-running tasks

domains.name: Evaluation
skills: Why evals: regression safety for prompt and model changes; building an eval set from real traffic
Grading methods: exact and programmatic checks, LLM-as-judge (rubrics, pairwise), human review
Judge pitfalls: position and verbosity bias, self-preference, calibration against human labels
Statistics for evals: sample size, confidence intervals, comparing two systems, flaky evals
Running evals in CI and production: online metrics, A/B tests, guardrail metrics and dashboards

domains.name: Production: cost, latency and reliability
skills: Cost modelling: input/output/cached tokens, batch discounts, per-feature unit economics
Latency: streaming, time to first token, prompt caching, smaller models, parallel calls
Reliability: rate limits, retries with backoff, timeouts, idempotency, provider fallbacks
Observability: tracing LLM calls and tool spans (OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions), logging prompts safely
Shipping safely: feature flags, shadow traffic, gradual rollout of model and prompt versions

domains.name: Security, safety and privacy
skills: Prompt injection: direct and indirect, why it cannot be fully filtered, and architectural defences
The OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications and how each shows up in real apps
Agent security: tool permissions, sandboxing, data exfiltration channels, human-in-the-loop approvals
Privacy and data handling: PII, retention, zero data retention options, tenant isolation in RAG
Content safety and guardrails: input and output filtering, refusals, and abuse monitoring
